source_text: Post has principales impatientiae materias ut potuimus regestas quid inter ceteras euagemur, quae domi, quae foris? lata atque diffusa est operatio mali multiplicia aspidum incitamenta, iaculantis, et modo paruula modo maxima. si paruula de sua mediocritate contemnas, maximis pro sua exuperantia cedas. ubi minor iniuria, ibi nulla necessitas impatientiae. at ubi maior iniuria, ibi necessarior iniuriae medela, patientia. certemus igitur quae a malo infliguntur sustinere, ut hostis studium aemulatio nostrae aequanimitatis eludat. si uero quaedam ipsi in nos aut imprudentia aut sponte etiam superducimus, aeque patienter obeamus quae nobis imputamus. quodsi a domino nonnulla credimus incuti, cui magis patientiam quam domino praebeamus? quin insuper gratulari [et gaudere] nos docet dignatione diuinae castigationis. ego, inquit, quos diligo castigo. o seruum illum beatum, cuius emendationi dominus instat, cui dignatur irasci, quem admonendi dissimulatione non decipit! undique igitur adstricti sumus officio patientiae administrandae, qua aequa ex parte aut erroribus nostris aut mali insidiis aut admonitionibus domini interuenimus. eius officii magna merces, felicitas scilicet. quos enim felices dominus nisi patientes nuncupauit dicendo: beati pauperes spiritu, illorum est enim regnum caelorum? nullus profecto spiritu pauper nisi humilis. quis autem humilis nisi patiens? quia nemo subicere sese potest sine prima patientia subiectionis ipsius. beati, inquit, flentes atque lugentes. quis talia sine patientia tolerat? itaque talibus et aduocatio et risus promittitur. beati mites. hoc quidem uocabulo impatientes non licet omnino censeri. item cum pacificos eodem titulo felicitatis notat et filios dei nuncupat, numquid impatientes pacis adfines? stultus hoc senserit. cum uero gaudete et exultate dicit, quotiens uos maledicent et persequentur, merces enim uestra plurima in caelo, id utique non [exultationis] impatientiae pollicetur, quia nemo in aduersis exultabit, nisi ante contempserit ea. nemo contemnet, nisi patientiam gesserit.
thought_title: Patience as the remedy for wrongs and the path to blessedness
orientation: Tertullian is continuing his argument that patience is the Christian response to every kind of wrong, now turning from revenge to the broader duty of enduring wrongs, divine correction, and the beatitudes.
pass_a_gloss: After these principal materials of impatience have been set down as we were able, why do we wander among the rest, which are at home, which are abroad? The operation of evil is wide and spread out, the manifold incitements of serpents, of the one hurling them, and now small, now very great. If you despise the small ones for their mediocrity, you may yield to the very great ones for their excess. Where the wrong is smaller, there is no necessity of impatience. But where the wrong is greater, there the remedy of the wrong is more necessary, patience. Let us strive therefore to endure the things which are inflicted by evil, so that the zeal of the enemy may be eluded by the rivalry of our equanimity. But if we ourselves bring certain things upon ourselves either through imprudence or even willingly, let us equally patiently undergo the things which we impute to ourselves. But if we believe that some things are inflicted by the Lord, to whom should we offer patience more than to the Lord? Moreover he teaches us to rejoice and be glad at the condescension of divine chastisement. I, he says, chastise those whom I love. O that blessed servant, upon whose correction the Lord insists, upon whom he deigns to be angry, whom he does not deceive by the concealment of admonition! Therefore on every side we are bound by the duty of administering patience, by which we meet equally either our own errors or the snares of evil or the admonitions of the Lord. The reward of this duty is great, namely happiness. For whom has the Lord called happy except the patient, saying: blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven? No one is certainly poor in spirit except the humble. But who is humble except the patient? Because no one can subject himself without the first patience of subjection itself. Blessed, he says, are those weeping and mourning. Who endures such things without patience? Therefore to such people both advocacy and laughter are promised. Blessed are the meek. By this name indeed the impatient are not permitted at all to be counted. Likewise when he marks the peacemakers with the same title of happiness and calls them sons of God, are the impatient at all neighbors of peace? A fool would think this. But when he says rejoice and exult, as often as they curse and persecute you, for your reward is very great in heaven, he certainly does not promise this to the impatience of exultation, because no one will exult in adversities unless he has first despised them. No one will despise them unless he has practiced patience.

pass_b_english: I have now set down the principal sources of impatience as best I could. Why should I wander among the rest, whether at home or abroad? The working of evil is wide and spread out. The serpent's manifold incitements hurl at us now small things, now the greatest. If they are small, you may despise them for their mediocrity. If they are greatest, you may yield to them for their excess. Where the wrong is smaller, there is no necessity for impatience. But where the wrong is greater, there the remedy for the wrong is more necessary: patience.

Let us strive, then, to endure what evil inflicts, so that our equanimity may elude the enemy's zeal. And if we ourselves bring certain things upon us, whether through imprudence or even willingly, let us equally bear patiently what we attribute to ourselves. But if we believe some things are inflicted by the Lord, to whom should we offer patience more than to the Lord? Moreover, he teaches us to rejoice and be glad in the condescension of divine chastisement. Scripture says, "I correct those whom I love" (Proverbs 3:12). O blessed servant, whose correction the Lord presses upon, whom he deigns to be angry with, whom he does not deceive by concealing his admonition!

On every side, then, we are bound to the duty of administering patience. Through it we meet equally our own errors, the snares of evil, or the admonitions of the Lord. The great reward of this duty is happiness, of course. For whom has the Lord called happy except the patient, saying, "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 5:3)? No one is poor in spirit unless humble. And who is humble unless patient? Because no one can subject himself without the prior patience of subjection itself.

The Lord says, "Blessed are those who weep and mourn" (Matthew 5:4). Who endures such things without patience? And so to such people both advocacy and laughter are promised. "Blessed are the meek" (Matthew 5:5). By this title the impatient cannot be counted at all. Likewise, when he marks the peacemakers with the same title of happiness and calls them sons of God (Matthew 5:9), are the impatient akin to peace? Only a fool would think so.

And when he says, "Rejoice and be glad whenever they curse and persecute you, for your reward is great in heaven" (Matthew 5:11-12), he certainly does not promise this to the impatience of exultation, because no one will exult in adversities unless he has first despised them. No one will despise them unless he has practiced patience.

problems.quote: so that our equanimity may mock the enemy's zeal.
problems.source_quote: ut hostis studium aemulatio nostrae aequanimitatis eludat.
problems.why: ‘eludat’ means ‘may elude/avoid’, not ‘mock’; the sense is changed.
problems.fix: so that our equanimity may elude the enemy's zeal.
problems.ruling: 'eludat' here means elude/evade, not mock; 'aemulatio' is our emulation, changing the sense.

edits.old: so that our equanimity may mock the enemy's zeal.
edits.new: so that our equanimity may elude the enemy's zeal.

fixed: Changed 'mock' to 'elude' to match 'eludat' in the source.

last_rejected.quote: so that our equanimity may elude the enemy's zeal
last_rejected.source_quote: ut hostis studium aemulatio nostrae aequanimitatis eludat
last_rejected.why: Subject is 'aemulatio' (emulation/zeal), not 'equanimity'; the enemy's zeal envies our calm and is eluded by it.
last_rejected.fix: so that our equanimity may elude the enemy's envious zeal
last_rejected.ruling: Latin: 'ut hostis studium ... eludat' makes enemy's zeal the object to be eluded; English makes equanimity the subject, but meaning (equanimity counters enemy zeal) stays similar.

polish.changed: Clarified speakers and pronouns, corrected the Proverbs attribution to Scripture rather than a divine speech, and broke long sentences into natural modern rhythm while preserving every claim and quotation.
